events.name: Tulip Mania
events.summary: Dutch tulip bulb prices rose 2,000% in under a year before collapsing in days. A single rare tulip bulb sold for more than a skilled craftsman's annual salary. The market vanished almost overnight when buyers stopped appearing.
events.causes: Futures contracts on tulip bulbs were traded by people who had never seen the actual bulb. Scarcity of certain varieties, social status signaling, and fear of missing out drove prices to irrational heights.
events.investor_behavior_then: Ordinary Dutch citizens sold homes and businesses to speculate on tulip bulbs. The price was driven entirely by the belief that the next buyer would pay more — not by any fundamental value of the flower itself.
events.investor_behavior_now: Modern equivalents include bidding wars on NFT profile pictures, meme coin rallies, and retail investors piling into trending stocks or assets because the online community is buying them.
events.shared_behavior: Price rises far beyond utility or income value because community excitement, scarcity framing, and fear of missing out become the only drivers.
events.why_similar: Both involve assets with limited or no income-producing value being priced purely on social momentum, scarcity narrative, and the expectation that demand will continue.
events.why_different: Some modern digital assets have actual network utility, programmable smart contracts, or payments infrastructure. The tulip had none. The collapse was also more contained geographically.
events.what_happened_after: The tulip market collapsed in February 1637. Prices fell 90%+ in weeks. Many speculative contracts were simply canceled. The Dutch economy survived because tulips were a small part of the broader economy — most of the damage was absorbed by individual speculators.
events.history_warning: When the only reason to buy is that the next buyer will pay more, the music always stops. The last buyers hold worthless assets.
events.personal_impact: In modern terms: people who bought meme coins or NFTs at peak prices with savings or borrowed money lost most or all of it. The damage concentrates on retail buyers who arrived last.

events.name: South Sea Bubble
events.summary: The South Sea Company promised to convert British government debt into company shares and profit from exclusive trade rights with South America. The company had almost no actual trade revenue. Share prices rose 1,000% before collapsing 85%, wiping out fortunes including Isaac Newton's.
events.causes: The company's narrative was compelling but the business fundamentals were fiction. Government officials held shares and promoted the stock. Parliament even passed laws to crush competing investments.
events.investor_behavior_then: Aristocrats, politicians, and ordinary citizens borrowed money to buy shares based on a story — exclusive trade monopoly, government backing, certain profits. Even Isaac Newton lost a fortune saying 'I can calculate the motion of heavenly bodies but not the madness of people.'
events.investor_behavior_now: Investors in SPACs, early crypto projects, AI startups, and speculative biotech often invest in the story before seeing revenue. Government endorsement or famous-person involvement amplifies belief.
events.shared_behavior: A compelling narrative backed by authority or social proof draws capital before any real earnings exist. The story becomes the investment thesis.
events.why_similar: Both involve buying into future promises supported by official-seeming backing, where the financial reality cannot support the narrative. Story-driven bubbles attract the most capital just before they collapse.
events.why_different: Today's markets have disclosure requirements, SEC enforcement, and short-sellers who can publicly challenge narratives. The South Sea Bubble operated with essentially no regulatory oversight.
events.what_happened_after: The collapse in 1720 caused one of England's first financial panics. Parliament passed the Bubble Act banning most corporate share issuance for over a century. The crash accelerated the separation of legitimate business from speculative finance.
events.history_warning: A powerful story backed by apparent authority can drive prices far beyond any reasonable future earnings. But stories cannot repay loans or produce dividends.
events.personal_impact: People who borrowed money to buy shares — a common practice — lost everything. Today's equivalent is buying speculative assets on margin or with credit cards.
timeline_now: Valuations exceed any reasonable future earnings

events.name: Railroad Expansion
events.summary: Railroads transformed the American economy, connecting coasts and creating national markets. The government gave railroad companies millions of acres of land grants. Investors poured in. The railroad industry saw three major speculative booms and busts between 1845 and 1893, including a massive collapse that triggered the Panic of 1893.
events.causes: Real transformative technology attracted legitimate investment, but also massive speculation. Overbuilding led to hundreds of railroads competing on the same routes. Easy credit and land grants encouraged over-expansion.
events.investor_behavior_then: Investors assumed that because railroads were real and transformative, every railroad would profit. Capital flooded in indiscriminately — financing both excellent routes and economically absurd ones. The underlying technology was real; the valuations were not.
events.investor_behavior_now: Today's AI infrastructure boom mirrors this pattern. Investors assume that because AI is real and transformative, every company with 'AI' in its name or strategy will profit. Capital flows to power companies, data centers, chip makers, and AI software without distinction.
events.shared_behavior: A truly transformative technology exists. Capital floods in faster than returns can justify. Overbuilding follows. Consolidation is inevitable. The technology survives; many companies do not.
events.why_similar: Both periods required massive physical infrastructure investment before the full economic payoff was visible. Government policy supported the buildout. The 'picks and shovels' companies — suppliers to the main trend — attracted enormous capital.
events.why_different: Software and AI infrastructure can scale much faster than physical rail. The marginal cost of copying software approaches zero, unlike steel track. AI also has no physical geography constraint. The boom-bust cycle may be faster.
events.what_happened_after: The railroad industry was real and transformative. The US economy was permanently changed. But most railroad companies eventually went bankrupt, consolidated, or were nationalized. The long-term winners were industrial companies that used the railroads — not necessarily the railroads themselves.
events.history_warning: The technology that changes the world does not guarantee profits for every company that builds it. Infrastructure tends to be overbuilt; competition drives down margins; survivors are few.
events.personal_impact: Workers in railroad boomtowns lost jobs when lines consolidated or failed. The same pattern applies to towns that bet everything on one employer or one industry trend.
timeline_now: AI demand drives chip and power investment
Consolidation — a few platform companies win

events.name: California Gold Rush
events.summary: 300,000 people flooded California seeking gold after the discovery at Sutter's Mill. Most individual miners made little. The biggest profits went to companies selling picks, shovels, blue jeans, food, and banking services to miners — not to the miners themselves.
events.causes: A credible discovery of real value triggered irrational migration. Social proof — everyone else is going — overrode cost-benefit analysis for most participants.
events.investor_behavior_then: Most gold seekers spent more on travel, supplies, and living costs than they ever recovered in gold. The people who reliably profited — Levi Strauss, Wells Fargo, general stores — sold things to the miners.
events.investor_behavior_now: The AI boom follows the same 'picks and shovels' pattern. NVIDIA profits more reliably from AI than most AI companies themselves. Power companies, cooling system makers, and data center REITs are selling supplies to the AI miners.
events.shared_behavior: When everyone rushes toward a new opportunity, the infrastructure suppliers often capture more value than the primary participants. The 'picks and shovels' business is more predictable than the underlying bet.
events.why_similar: The pattern of infrastructure providers profiting more reliably than end-users of a technology boom is one of the most repeated patterns in economic history.
events.why_different: In the Gold Rush, gold was finite and physically exhaustible. AI is a software capability that can be reproduced and improved indefinitely. The total market is not constrained by a physical resource.
events.what_happened_after: California was transformed. The Gold Rush built cities, financial systems, and infrastructure. But most individual gold seekers returned east no richer than they left. The lasting winners built services around the boom.
events.history_warning: Everyone rushing to the gold does not mean everyone will find it. The reliable profit is often in what the gold seekers need, not the gold itself.
events.personal_impact: Families sold farms and businesses to fund cross-country trips for gold that often did not materialize. Modern equivalent: quitting a job to trade crypto full-time or build an AI startup with no business model.
timeline_then: Individual mining becomes competitive and unprofitable
Mining fades but California infrastructure remains
timeline_now: NVIDIA, power companies, data centers profit first
Most AI applications struggle to monetize

events.name: 1929 Margin Speculation
events.summary: American stock prices rose 500% in the 1920s, largely fueled by buying stocks on 10:1 margin — meaning investors put down only 10% of the purchase price. The crash began October 1929 and triggered the Great Depression. The Dow took 25 years to recover to its 1929 peak.
events.causes: Cheap margin credit, radio euphoria about permanent prosperity, and the belief that a 'new era' of technology had eliminated the business cycle. Sound familiar?
events.investor_behavior_then: Banks and brokerages encouraged customers to buy stocks on credit. Ordinary workers invested life savings in margin accounts. The prevailing belief was that the stock market could only go up — a new era had arrived.
events.investor_behavior_now: Record margin debt levels, zero-commission trading driving retail participation, and beliefs that AI or crypto represent permanent paradigm shifts show similar dynamics.
events.shared_behavior: Easy credit conditions lead to leveraged speculation. Leverage amplifies gains on the way up and creates cascading forced selling on the way down. The higher the leverage, the worse the collapse.
events.why_similar: High leverage, new-era thinking, and overvalued markets driven by a real underlying trend are the same combination that preceded 1929.
events.why_different: Today's Federal Reserve has tools Hoover did not — emergency lending, deposit insurance, QE. Modern crashes are more likely to produce brutal bear markets than decade-long depressions. The safety net is real, though not unlimited.
events.what_happened_after: The market fell 89% over three years. Unemployment reached 25%. Banks failed. The Roosevelt administration redesigned the entire financial system: Glass-Steagall, the SEC, deposit insurance, Social Security. The modern financial regulatory framework exists because of 1929.
events.history_warning: Leverage turns a painful correction into a catastrophe. Assets bought with borrowed money must be sold when prices fall, turning a selloff into a crash.
events.personal_impact: People who bought stocks on margin in 1929 not only lost their investment — they owed the balance of their margin loans to banks that were also failing. Losing more than 100% of what you put in is the leverage trap.

events.name: 1970s Oil Shocks
events.summary: The Arab oil embargo of 1973 and the Iranian Revolution in 1979 caused oil prices to quadruple then double again. Inflation exceeded 14%. The Federal Reserve raised rates to 20% under Paul Volcker to kill inflation — triggering back-to-back recessions in 1980 and 1981-82.
events.causes: OPEC's political leverage over oil supply gave producing nations the ability to trigger a supply shock. US dependence on imported oil made the economy uniquely vulnerable. Government price controls made shortages worse.
events.investor_behavior_then: Investors fled growth stocks and rushed into commodities, gold, and energy. The Nifty Fifty — America's blue-chip darlings — collapsed as high inflation destroyed their valuation multiples. Savings accounts paying 17% pulled capital from stocks.
events.investor_behavior_now: Today's oil shocks from the Russia-Ukraine war and Middle East tensions echo the 1970s. But the US is now a net oil exporter, reducing vulnerability. The inflation impact on consumer spending and Fed policy is the most direct parallel.
events.shared_behavior: Geopolitical control over critical energy supplies creates inflation that forces central banks into painful choices between growth and price stability.
events.why_similar: Energy supply shocks feed inflation, which forces the Fed to raise rates, which slows the economy, which raises unemployment — the same chain observed in the 1970s.
events.why_different: The US is now the world's largest oil producer, fundamentally reducing the leverage OPEC held in 1973. The energy transition is also diversifying the supply away from any single geopolitical source.
events.what_happened_after: Volcker's rate hikes succeeded in killing inflation but caused painful recessions. Energy efficiency improved dramatically. Nuclear power expanded. The crisis accelerated investment in alternative energy. By the mid-1980s, oil prices collapsed as new supply came online.
events.history_warning: Energy is the price of everything. When oil prices rise, groceries, shipping, manufacturing, and heating all become more expensive. Inflation from energy shocks is especially hard to control without causing economic pain.
events.personal_impact: Gas lines in 1973 meant Americans could only fill up on odd or even days based on license plate numbers. Higher oil prices raised the cost of every product shipped by truck. Today: gas prices affect every household's monthly budget.
timeline_now: Russia invades Ukraine, energy prices surge

events.name: Japanese Asset Bubble
events.summary: Japanese real estate and stock prices rose 400%+ in five years. The Imperial Palace grounds in Tokyo were estimated to be worth more than all of California. The Nikkei stock index peaked in December 1989 at 38,916. It did not return to that level until 2024 — 35 years later.
events.causes: Easy monetary policy, bank overlending against real estate collateral, a strong yen reducing export competitiveness, and government policies creating asset price inflation all contributed. Banks lent against inflated collateral that further inflated collateral in a self-reinforcing cycle.
events.investor_behavior_then: Japanese corporations bought trophy properties in New York, Hawaii, and Los Angeles. Ordinary Japanese citizens assumed real estate would always rise. Banks approved loans based on inflated land valuations. The economy ran on asset price appreciation as its growth model.
events.investor_behavior_now: Post-2020 US real estate markets showed similar dynamics in many cities — bidding wars, prices rising 30-40%, buyers waiving inspections. Commercial real estate office sector faces a structural shift akin to Japan's retail real estate after the bubble.
events.shared_behavior: When banks lend against rising assets, and rising assets attract more lending, the cycle is self-reinforcing until it isn't. Rising interest rates or falling demand can pop the collateral chain.
events.why_similar: Bank lending cycles tied to asset prices, easy monetary policy creating speculative conditions, and demographic shifts are the closest modern parallels.
events.why_different: Japan had unique structural issues: keiretsu corporate cross-shareholding, a highly homogeneous domestic economy, and a rapidly aging population that worsened the decades of stagnation. The US economy is more dynamic and demographically diverse.
events.what_happened_after: Japan entered two lost decades. The Nikkei didn't recover for 35 years. Banks wrote off trillions in bad loans. Deflation became entrenched. The lesson became a textbook case in monetary policy and financial stability.
events.history_warning: When an entire economy is built on rising asset prices, the inevitable correction doesn't just hurt speculators — it cripples the banks that lent against those assets, which then stops lending to businesses, which creates unemployment, which creates more defaults.
events.personal_impact: Japanese workers who bought homes at peak prices in 1989 spent their entire careers paying mortgages on properties worth a fraction of what they paid. Negative equity for a generation.
timeline_then: Banks fail, deflation begins, lost decades

events.name: Dot-Com Bubble
events.summary: Technology stocks rose 400% from 1995 to March 2000. The NASDAQ lost 78% of its value by October 2002. Companies like Pets.com spent $11M on Super Bowl ads and went bankrupt nine months later. But the survivors — Amazon, Google, Apple — went on to become the most valuable companies in history.
events.causes: The internet was genuinely transformative. But investors assumed every internet company would be profitable, ignored cash burn, and bid valuations to levels that required decades of perfect execution to justify. 'Eyeballs' replaced revenue as the metric that mattered.
events.investor_behavior_then: IPO day gains of 100-300% were common. Day traders quit jobs to trade stocks full time. Venture capital flowed to companies with no revenue model. Businesses burned cash to build user bases assuming monetization would follow.
events.investor_behavior_now: AI companies are attracting investment regardless of revenue. Some AI startups have raised hundreds of millions before generating meaningful income. The language has shifted — 'AI-powered' has become the new 'dot-com.' But major AI companies do have real revenues today.
events.shared_behavior: A genuinely transformative technology attracts speculative capital that cannot distinguish between real opportunities and hype. Valuations disconnect from any reasonable earnings projection.
events.why_similar: Genuinely transformative technology, new-era thinking dismissing traditional valuation, venture capital and institutional capital flowing before business models are proven, and mainstream media attention driving retail participation.
events.why_different: The major AI companies (Microsoft, Google, Nvidia, Meta) already generate hundreds of billions in revenue. In 1999, many top internet companies had no revenue at all. The speculative risk today is more concentrated in smaller, pre-revenue AI startups — not the platform companies.
events.what_happened_after: The internet changed the world exactly as promised. But most internet companies failed. The survivors — Amazon (down 94% in the crash), Apple, Google — took years to recover. An investor who bought the NASDAQ at peak in 2000 waited until 2015 to break even.
events.history_warning: The technology that wins may not be the company that wins. Buying high because the technology is real is not the same as buying undervalued assets.
events.personal_impact: Millions of employees saw stock options worth millions on paper become worthless. Retirement accounts invested in tech funds lost 70-80%. Companies that planned future IPOs were stranded without funding.
timeline_now: Some AI companies lack clear revenue models

events.name: 2008 Housing Crisis
events.summary: US housing prices rose 124% from 1997 to 2006. Banks packaged subprime mortgages into complex securities and sold them globally. When housing prices fell, the entire global financial system nearly collapsed. The S&P 500 fell 57%. Unemployment reached 10%.
events.causes: Deregulation allowed banks to originate mortgages without keeping the risk — they sold it to Wall Street. Wall Street packaged risky loans with safe ones and sold the bundles globally. Rating agencies gave AAA ratings to junk. Everyone had incentive to keep the machine going.
events.investor_behavior_then: Homebuyers took on mortgages they could not afford because prices 'always go up.' Banks approved NINJA loans — No Income, No Job, No Assets. Investors assumed housing was a one-way trade. The risk was passed so many times it became invisible.
events.investor_behavior_now: Commercial real estate faces potential structural impairment from remote work permanently reducing office demand. Regional banks hold significant CRE loans. Consumer debt (credit cards, auto loans) is at record levels. BNPL extends credit to borderline borrowers in ways that echo subprime auto loans.
events.shared_behavior: When assets are bought primarily on leverage and the assumption of ever-rising prices, the eventual reset of those prices triggers a credit crisis that affects far more than just the speculators.
events.why_similar: Commercial real estate, consumer credit, and regional bank exposure to real estate echo some structural vulnerabilities of 2004-2008. BNPL and auto loan delinquency rates are rising.
events.why_different: Residential mortgage standards are dramatically tighter post-Dodd-Frank. Major bank capital ratios are much higher. There is no systemic securitization of subprime mortgages on a 2007 scale. The risk today is more concentrated in commercial real estate and consumer credit.
events.what_happened_after: The government bailed out major banks. Dodd-Frank redesigned the regulatory system. The Fed created entirely new tools — QE, bank stress tests. Housing prices recovered and then exceeded pre-crash levels. But 10 million families lost their homes.
events.history_warning: When credit is easy and assets always seem to rise, risk is being hidden, not eliminated. Leverage on real assets always has a clearing price.
events.personal_impact: Ten million Americans lost their homes to foreclosure. Millions more lost retirement savings. The median household took 10 years to recover to 2007 net worth levels. The damage to middle-class wealth was the most severe in 80 years.
timeline_now: System more resilient but stress areas exist

events.name: Cold War Defense Spending Cycle
events.summary: The Cold War created 40 years of sustained defense spending that built companies like Lockheed, Boeing, Raytheon, and General Dynamics into industrial giants. Congressional appropriations, not market competition, determined winners. Companies with strong political relationships and contract networks thrived regardless of commercial performance.
events.causes: The existential fear of Soviet nuclear capability ensured bipartisan political support for defense spending across administrations. Technology competition — space race, ICBM development, fighter aircraft — required long-term investment.
events.investor_behavior_then: Defense stocks were considered stable, dividend-paying, recession-resistant investments. The risk was political — contract cancellation or political shift could hurt specific companies. But overall spending was guaranteed.
events.investor_behavior_now: NATO defense budget increases following Russia's invasion of Ukraine, Middle East conflicts, and the China-Taiwan risk have created a new structural defense spending cycle. The same dynamic applies: government contracts, not market competition, determine the winners.
events.shared_behavior: Geopolitical threat perception drives political consensus on defense spending regardless of party. Companies with strong government relationships — and politicians who direct contracts to those companies — benefit most reliably.
events.why_similar: The structural driver — geopolitical threat requiring government defense spending — is the same. Congressional defense appropriations follow threat perception, not budget discipline.
events.why_different: Modern warfare also includes cyber, space, drones, and AI warfare — sectors that did not exist in the Cold War. Defense spending is now more technologically diverse, and new entrants like Palantir and SpaceX have changed who captures the contracts.
events.what_happened_after: When the Cold War ended and the Berlin Wall fell, defense stocks lagged significantly for nearly a decade as the 'peace dividend' was harvested. The boom restarted after 9/11 and has continued with escalating global tensions.
events.history_warning: Defense stocks are driven by political will to spend, not by commercial market forces. A change in political priorities — a peace deal, a budget crisis, an election — can rapidly alter the outlook regardless of company performance.
events.personal_impact: Military towns — San Diego, Norfolk, Huntsville — experience economic cycles tied directly to defense budget cycles. When spending falls, local economies suffer. When it rises, they boom.
timeline_now: AI warfare, drones, cyber add new categories

events.name: COVID Crash and Recovery
events.summary: The S&P 500 fell 34% in 33 days — the fastest bear market in history. The US government and Federal Reserve injected $5+ trillion in stimulus. Markets fully recovered in 5 months and kept rising for 18 more months. The lasting consequence was the worst inflation in 40 years.
events.causes: A global pandemic shut the economy. The government response — sending money directly to households, funding payroll protection, buying corporate bonds — was unprecedented in speed and scale.
events.investor_behavior_then: Investors who sold in March 2020 were badly wrong. Markets recovered faster than any historical precedent. Retail trading surged as bored workers at home opened brokerage accounts. Meme stocks, crypto, and SPACs all boomed in the cheap-money environment.
events.investor_behavior_now: The post-COVID era IS the current market. The inflation, interest rates, housing prices, and market valuations we live with today are the direct consequence of 2020 stimulus. Understanding COVID is understanding today.
events.shared_behavior: Massive fiscal and monetary stimulus creates asset price inflation followed by consumer price inflation. The unwinding of that stimulus — rate hikes — is always painful.
events.why_similar: COVID is the most directly relevant historical parallel to today's economic environment because today's conditions ARE the aftermath of COVID.
events.why_different: COVID's unique feature was combining supply shock (factories shut), demand shock (no spending options), and then massive demand stimulus (checks to households) simultaneously. This triple combination had no modern precedent.
events.what_happened_after: The stimulus worked to prevent depression but created 9% inflation. The Fed's rate hiking cycle from 0% to 5.5% was the fastest in decades. Housing became unaffordable for many first-time buyers. The economy avoided recession but many Americans felt financially worse despite rising asset prices.
events.history_warning: The money created by stimulus does not disappear — it lives in asset prices and eventually in consumer prices. Every dollar printed today becomes someone's inflation bill tomorrow.
events.personal_impact: Renters and first-time homebuyers experienced the most pain — assets they don't own rose in price while their earnings did not keep pace. Homeowners with mortgages locked in at 3% are insulated. Those trying to buy face 7%+ rates.
timeline_then: Fed cuts to zero, buys bonds

events.name: Meme Stock Mania
events.summary: Reddit's WallStreetBets community coordinated to squeeze hedge fund short positions in GameStop, AMC, and BlackBerry. GameStop rose 1,700% in weeks. Several hedge funds lost billions. Robinhood restricted trading, triggering a congressional hearing. Most buyers who did not exit near the top lost most of their money.
events.causes: Zero-commission trading, smartphone apps, COVID boredom, stimulus checks, and a Reddit community identifying heavily shorted stocks created a perfect environment for coordinated short squeezes.
events.investor_behavior_then: Young retail investors felt like they were beating Wall Street at its own game. The community celebrated gains and encouraged holding even as prices collapsed. 'Diamond hands' became a rallying cry that kept people holding through 80% drawdowns.
events.investor_behavior_now: The meme stock dynamic still exists. Social media can rapidly coordinate buying in heavily shorted stocks. Crypto meme coins show the same pattern. The mechanism is real — short squeezes happen — but the question is always who is holding when the squeeze ends.
events.shared_behavior: Community identity and shared narrative override individual financial analysis. Holding becomes a tribal statement, not an investment decision.
events.why_similar: Any heavily shorted, low-float asset can be subject to coordinated buying pressure from social communities. The psychological mechanism — belonging + FOMO + anti-establishment sentiment — is repeatable.
events.why_different: Regulatory attention has increased. Brokerages have added restrictions. Short interest in popular stocks is now monitored more carefully. The pure surprise element that made January 2021 so violent is harder to replicate at the same scale.
events.what_happened_after: GameStop fell 90% from peak. Most retail buyers lost money. Congress held hearings but passed no major legislation. Robinhood's IPO underperformed. The hedge funds adjusted their short positioning approaches. A smaller recurring meme stock phenomenon persists.
events.history_warning: A community rallying behind a trade can create short-term forced buying that looks like fundamental price discovery but is not. When the squeeze ends, the price has nowhere to go but down.
events.personal_impact: Millions of retail investors who bought GameStop near its peak lost most of their investment. Some borrowed money or invested emergency funds. The financial damage was concentrated on those who arrived after institutional money had already exited.
timeline_now: Crypto meme coins show same pattern

events.name: Crypto Boom and Bust
events.summary: Bitcoin rose from $1,000 to $20,000 in 2017, crashed 84%, rose to $69,000 in 2021, crashed 77% to $16,000. FTX's $32B collapse in November 2022 was the largest crypto fraud since Madoff. Bitcoin recovered to record highs above $100,000 in 2025 driven by spot ETF approvals and institutional adoption.
events.causes: Multiple cycles with different drivers: 2017 was pure retail speculation. 2020-2021 added institutional adoption and DeFi. 2022 collapsed from overleveraged funds, algorithmic stablecoins, and fraud. 2024-2025 recovery is driven by real institutional capital via ETFs and regulatory clarity.
events.investor_behavior_then: In 2017: everyone at Thanksgiving was asking how to buy Bitcoin. In 2021: DeFi protocols offering 100%+ annual yields attracted capital that had no idea what the risks were. In 2022: institutional leverage products amplified the collapse.
events.investor_behavior_now: Bitcoin is now accessible via ETFs in retirement accounts. Institutional investors include BlackRock and Fidelity. The asset class is maturing but speculation in altcoins and meme coins continues to show 2017-style behavior.
events.shared_behavior: Each crypto cycle attracts more institutional participation and more regulatory clarity, while the speculative fringe continues to show classic bubble behavior in newer tokens and projects.
events.why_similar: The speculation-to-maturation pattern in crypto mirrors early equity market development. Every new asset class begins in speculation and — if it survives — moves toward institutionalization.
events.why_different: The 2024 Bitcoin recovery is fundamentally different from 2017 — driven by BlackRock's ETF approval, not retail FOMO. Bitcoin has achieved a level of institutional legitimacy that most 2017 tokens never reached.
events.what_happened_after: Bitcoin has survived four 80%+ crashes and recovered to new highs each time. Most altcoins from 2017 are worth essentially nothing. The technology persists; most tokens created on top of it do not.
events.history_warning: Crypto cycles amplify both gains and losses. The difference between Bitcoin and altcoins is increasingly the difference between the railroad and a specific railroad company — one survives, most others fail.
events.personal_impact: People who invested life savings in crypto at peaks — particularly in 2017 and 2021 — and did not exit experienced 70-80% losses that took years to recover or never recovered. Diversification and position sizing matter enormously in high-volatility assets.

events.name: NFT Mania
events.summary: Non-fungible tokens — digital files with blockchain ownership records — sold for hundreds of millions. The Bored Ape Yacht Club collection saw floor prices rise to $400,000 per image. Most NFT collections are now worth under 1% of peak value. The market went from $17 billion in volume in 2021 to under $100 million by 2023.
events.causes: Zero-cost digital reproduction made physical scarcity irrelevant, so NFTs created artificial blockchain-enforced scarcity. Celebrity endorsement, community membership, and speculation on resale value drove prices.
events.investor_behavior_then: NFT buyers often didn't understand what they were buying — a certificate of 'ownership' of a JPEG that anyone could copy. The value was in community membership, status signaling, and the expectation of resale at higher prices.
events.investor_behavior_now: The NFT market has nearly completely collapsed. This pattern mirrors Beanie Baby mania — the controlled scarcity argument was real, but it couldn't sustain price appreciation when attention moved elsewhere.
events.shared_behavior: Artificial scarcity + status signaling + celebrity endorsement + active secondary market creates price bubbles in assets with no income or utility. When attention fades, the only remaining question is who is holding when the music stops.
events.why_similar: NFT mania is the most direct modern equivalent of tulip mania and Beanie Baby speculation — assets purchased purely as stores of status and resale expectation rather than utility or income.
events.why_different: Blockchain technology could eventually enable legitimate use cases for digital ownership in gaming, real estate, and credentials. The NFT mania destroyed credibility for legitimate uses, but the underlying technology has real potential applications.
events.what_happened_after: 99%+ of NFT collections have lost essentially all of their value. OpenSea's trading volume fell 99% from peak. Celebrity NFT endorsers faced class action lawsuits. The sector effectively collapsed, though niche use cases persisted.
events.history_warning: Digital scarcity is a useful concept. But an artificially scarce JPEG of an ape has no income, no utility, and no fundamental floor value. When the community moves on, the price returns to its intrinsic value.
events.personal_impact: People who bought NFTs with retirement savings or borrowed money suffered real financial losses. Some celebrities who promoted NFTs without disclosing financial relationships faced SEC scrutiny and legal action.
timeline_now: NFT market essentially defunct for speculation
Legitimate blockchain ownership use cases developing

events.name: EV Mania
events.summary: Tesla rose 740% in 2020. Dozens of EV startups went public via SPACs with no revenue. Rivian debuted with a $150B market cap with a handful of trucks produced. By 2023, most EV startups had collapsed or were fighting for survival. The technology is real but the valuations were irrational.
events.causes: Climate urgency, government subsidies, Tesla's success, and SPAC mania created an environment where any EV story could raise hundreds of millions regardless of manufacturing readiness.
events.investor_behavior_then: Investors assumed EV would be a winner-takes-most market like software, pricing Tesla as the only survivor. EV startups raised billions before producing a single car. The analogy to software — zero marginal cost — was wrong for physical manufacturing.
events.investor_behavior_now: The AI boom shows some similar dynamics — assuming software winner-takes-most logic applies to hardware-dependent AI infrastructure. AI data centers are more like factories than software companies.
events.shared_behavior: New technology with real government support and genuine market opportunity attracts more capital than the total addressable market can support. Competition turns an opportunity into a margin-crushing race to the bottom.
events.why_similar: Technology transition boom with government subsidy support, early mover advantage assumptions that didn't materialize, and capital markets funding competitors faster than the market could grow.
events.why_different: EVs are physical manufactured goods competing against legacy automakers with manufacturing expertise, supply chains, and distribution. Software AI is more scalable. But the competitive dynamics in AI chips, models, and infrastructure increasingly resemble EV — many well-funded competitors, margin compression possible.
events.what_happened_after: Tesla survived and remained dominant. Rivian and Lucid traded far below their peak valuations. Fisker went bankrupt. Chinese EV makers (BYD) turned out to be the most competitive threat. The EV market is growing but the investment returns have been poor for most participants outside of Tesla.
events.history_warning: The transition is real. Not every company making the transition vehicle is a good investment. In manufacturing, execution and cost discipline matter more than first-mover narrative.
events.personal_impact: EV buyers benefited from government tax credits. The broader energy transition created jobs in battery manufacturing. But workers in ICE vehicle manufacturing faced structural employment risk.
timeline_then: Most EV startups fail or struggle 2022-2024
timeline_now: NVIDIA as the only consistent winner

events.name: SPAC Mania
events.summary: Special Purpose Acquisition Companies raised $163 billion in 2020 alone. SPACs allowed companies to go public without traditional SEC disclosure requirements. Most SPAC-acquired companies significantly underperformed the market. The SPAC ETF fell 70% from peak.
events.causes: Low interest rates, retail trading boom, and regulations that allowed aggressive forward projections in SPAC prospectuses but not traditional IPOs. Banks earned fees on both sides of the transaction.
events.investor_behavior_then: Celebrities, athletes, and politicians launched SPACs. Retail investors bought in because famous names were attached. The underlying businesses often had no revenue and aggressive 5-year projections that replaced actual financials.
events.investor_behavior_now: SPACs still exist but on a dramatically smaller scale. The same psychology — investing in a story before fundamentals exist — persists in AI startups and pre-revenue tech companies now raising at large valuations.
events.shared_behavior: Financial instruments that lower disclosure requirements and allow creative financial storytelling attract capital that would be redirected if standard analysis were applied.
events.why_similar: The story-before-revenue pattern in SPACs mirrors AI startup investment where projected TAM and 5-year model assumptions substitute for current financial performance.
events.why_different: AI companies going through traditional IPO processes face more scrutiny than SPACs did. The most successful AI companies (Anthropic, OpenAI) are private for longer, which filters out some of the worst quality-of-business issues that plagued SPACs.
events.what_happened_after: The SEC cracked down on SPAC accounting in 2022, requiring standard disclosure. SPAC volume collapsed. Most SPAC mergers traded significantly below the $10 IPO price. The space largely imploded.
events.history_warning: Financial instruments designed to reduce disclosure always attract both legitimate innovation and low-quality businesses that could not pass normal scrutiny. The ratio skews badly over time.
events.personal_impact: Retail investors who bought celebrity SPACs lost significant money. The names behind the SPACs rarely had fiduciary responsibility — they were sponsors and promoters, not actual business operators.
timeline_then: Most SPACs trade far below NAV
timeline_now: AI startups fill same narrative role

events.name: Coal to Oil Energy Transition
events.summary: Coal powered the Industrial Revolution. The discovery of oil and the internal combustion engine made coal-fired steam engines obsolete within decades. Coal companies that did not diversify were eventually left with stranded assets. Oil companies that rode the transition created Standard Oil — the most valuable company in history at its peak.
events.causes: Superior energy density of petroleum, the internal combustion engine, and wartime demand for oil created an irreversible transition. Infrastructure — roads, pipelines, refineries — locked in oil's advantage.
events.investor_behavior_then: Coal investors did not believe the transition would come fast enough to matter. Many doubled down. Standard Oil investors who stayed long became extraordinarily wealthy. The mistake was assuming incumbent technology would persist because of existing infrastructure.
events.investor_behavior_now: Today's energy transition from fossil fuels to renewables follows the same pattern. Fossil fuel companies with stranded asset risk, renewable energy companies fighting for position, and infrastructure companies caught in the transition all mirror 1900-1950 dynamics.
events.shared_behavior: The transition takes longer than optimists expect, moves faster than incumbents expect, and the winners are rarely the incumbents who try to adapt — more often the new entrants who build the new infrastructure from scratch.
events.why_similar: Energy infrastructure transitions create both enormous winners among new technology companies and severe long-term losses for incumbent companies that refuse to adapt or cannot adapt fast enough.
events.why_different: Fossil fuels still power 80% of global energy and have decades of use ahead. The renewable transition is slower, more politically contested, and more technologically complex than coal-to-oil. The endpoint may be similar but the timeline is much longer.
events.what_happened_after: Oil replaced coal as the dominant energy source within 50 years. Coal never disappeared — it remained dominant in electricity generation for decades — but its commercial and transportation dominance ended. Standard Oil became so powerful it was broken up by antitrust in 1911.
events.history_warning: Energy transitions always happen slower than advocates predict and faster than incumbents want to believe. The companies that control the new infrastructure always capture more value than the companies still optimizing the old infrastructure.
events.personal_impact: Coal mining communities experienced the same structural employment shock that oil and gas communities now fear from the energy transition. The jobs in new energy sectors often appear in different geographic areas than the jobs they replace.
timeline_then: Coal's dominance in transportation ends by 1940
timeline_now: Renewable costs fall below fossil fuels
Government mandates and subsidies accelerate transition
Stranded asset risk grows for fossil fuel infrastructure

events.name: AI Infrastructure Boom
events.summary: The launch of ChatGPT in November 2022 triggered the largest wave of technology investment in history. NVIDIA's market cap surpassed $3 trillion. Microsoft, Google, Meta, and Amazon are each spending $50B+ on AI infrastructure annually. The buildout resembles the railroad expansion, the internet buildout, and the electrification of America simultaneously.
events.causes: Large language model breakthroughs demonstrated transformative commercial applications for artificial intelligence. Every major corporation concluded that AI adoption was not optional — the competitive threat from non-adoption was perceived as existential.
events.investor_behavior_then: This IS the current event — not history yet. But the behavior mirrors every previous technology boom: capital floods in faster than returns can justify, 'AI' becomes a marketing term added to every company, and valuations price in a winner-takes-most outcome that rarely materializes across an entire industry.
events.investor_behavior_now: This is the current moment. NVIDIA has become the most valuable company in the world on the strength of AI chip demand. The question is not whether AI is transformative — it clearly is — but whether current valuations price in too much, too fast.
events.shared_behavior: Investors are repeating every historical technology boom: assuming the trend will be even bigger than it is, assuming current leaders will permanently dominate, and assuming rapid adoption timelines that historically prove optimistic.
events.why_similar: Railroad expansion, electrification, the internet, and AI all follow the same S-curve adoption pattern. The early phase overestimates near-term impact and underestimates long-term transformation.
events.why_different: AI may have a faster adoption curve than any previous technology because it operates through existing internet infrastructure — no physical installation required. The marginal cost of AI deployment is declining faster than the marginal cost of railroads or power lines.
events.what_happened_after: Still ongoing. History suggests that even when the technology wins, most companies exposed to the trend will disappoint investors who bought at peak excitement. The picks-and-shovels players (NVIDIA, power companies) will likely persist longer than pure-play AI software companies.
events.history_warning: Every technology that changed the world also destroyed most companies that tried to profit from it. The technology survives. The hype cycle does not.
events.personal_impact: AI will likely affect employment across almost every white-collar profession. The economic disruption from automation may be larger and faster than previous technology transitions because AI can perform cognitive work, not just physical or repetitive tasks.
timeline_then: Power grid capacity becomes critical constraint
timeline_now: Energy demand for data centers straining grids

events.name: Whaling Industry Collapse
events.summary: Whale oil powered America's lamps and lubricated its machinery before petroleum. New Bedford, Massachusetts was once the world's richest city per capita, built entirely on whaling. The discovery of petroleum in 1859 and kerosene's lower cost destroyed the whaling industry within 20 years. The last American whaling ship stopped sailing in 1927.
events.causes: A cheaper, more abundant substitute (kerosene from petroleum) eliminated demand for whale oil almost entirely within two decades. The transition was faster than the industry expected and left most participants with worthless assets.
events.investor_behavior_then: Whaling ship owners doubled down on the industry as oil prices began to fall, believing whaling would remain viable for some uses. Most were wrong. The industry did not slowly decline — it collapsed.
events.investor_behavior_now: Oil and gas companies facing the energy transition risk experiencing a similar dynamic. The question is whether renewables will disrupt fossil fuels as suddenly as petroleum disrupted whale oil, or whether the transition takes multiple decades.
events.shared_behavior: Dominant resource industries facing new substitute technologies often fail to react adequately because the threat seems distant, then becomes sudden. The assets built for the old technology become liabilities overnight.
events.why_similar: Any dominant energy source or resource industry facing a cheaper, more abundant substitute will follow this pattern. The lesson is relevant for coal, oil, and any company with large capital tied to a resource that has a substitute.
events.why_different: Fossil fuels are far more embedded in global infrastructure than whale oil ever was. The transition away from oil and gas will take decades, not 20 years. The stranded asset risk is real but the timeline is much longer.
events.what_happened_after: New Bedford never recovered its 19th-century prosperity. The whaling ports became museums. The capital tied up in whaling ships was completely lost. The petroleum industry that replaced it created far more wealth.
events.history_warning: When a better substitute exists, the speed of replacement is almost always faster than the incumbent industry expects. Stranded asset risk is real and permanent.
events.personal_impact: Entire communities built around whaling — New Bedford, Nantucket, Sag Harbor — experienced permanent economic disruption. Today's oil towns face a distant but potentially similar structural risk.
timeline_then: Kerosene costs less than whale oil
timeline_now: Renewable energy costs below fossil fuels in many markets
Stranded asset risk growing for coal first

events.name: Black Monday 1987
events.summary: The S&P 500 fell 20.5% in a single day — still the largest single-day percentage decline in US market history. Portfolio insurance strategies, designed to protect investors, became the mechanism that amplified the crash. Algorithmic selling triggered more selling in a cascade that human intervention could not stop.
events.causes: Portfolio insurance strategies used futures contracts to automatically sell equity exposure as prices fell — in theory, limiting downside. In practice, all these systems sold simultaneously, amplifying the decline. Market makers could not absorb the volume.
events.investor_behavior_then: The crash happened so fast that individual investors could not react. The automated systems that were supposed to protect portfolios caused the crash. It was the first major demonstration that automated trading could damage markets rather than improve them.
events.investor_behavior_now: Algorithmic trading now represents 60-70% of US equity volume. Correlated algorithmic strategies can trigger flash crashes. The August 2024 VIX spike demonstrated that automated deleveraging can amplify moves dramatically. Market structure risk is higher now than in 1987 in some respects.
events.shared_behavior: When correlated automated strategies all trigger simultaneously, market liquidity disappears and prices overshoot in ways that have nothing to do with fundamental value.
events.why_similar: Modern algorithmic trading, risk parity funds, and volatility targeting strategies all create the potential for correlated selling cascades that amplify corrections into crashes.
events.why_different: The Fed has circuit breakers, the NYSE has trading halts, and there are mechanisms to interrupt feedback loops that did not exist in 1987. However, these mechanisms have never been tested in a genuine systemic stress event comparable to 1929 or 2008.
events.what_happened_after: Markets recovered fully within 2 years. The economy did not fall into recession. The Fed under Greenspan provided liquidity. Circuit breakers were introduced. The crash taught markets that automated selling could be self-defeating — though the lesson has to be relearned periodically.
events.history_warning: When everyone runs the same hedge at the same time, the hedge becomes the problem. Automated risk management amplifies moves when it matters most.
events.personal_impact: Investors who panicked and sold on October 20, 1987 crystallized losses. Those who held recovered fully within 2 years. The lesson repeated in COVID 2020 — markets that crash fast can recover fast.
timeline_now: Correlated positioning in momentum and quality factors
